newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's Kim signals policy shift over labour law.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Kim signals policy shift over labour law.

text.p: President Kim Young-sam signalled a major turnaround on Monday by offering to meet opposition leaders for talks on a new labour law, and prosecutors said they would delay the arrest of fugitive union leaders.
"President Kim will meet leaders of political parties represented in parliament to discuss the current situation tomorrow (Tuesday)," a presidential spokesman told reporters.
Kim has previously ruled out such a meeting, insisting he would neither scrap the law or revise it.
The South Korean leader's softening stand coincided with the return to work on Monday by strikers after union leaders called off indefinite stoppages at the weekend.
It was the first day of normal production since the strikes began on December 26 after the ruling New Korea Party rammed the labour bill through parliament.
Spokesman Park Hong-yeop of the main opposition National Congress for New Politics welcomed the talks offer.
"We, of course, will attend the meeting," he said. "Our party's basic position is that the labour bill must be reviewed in parliament."
Because of the thaw, a senior state prosecutor said, the arrests of the seven leaders of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions holed up at Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral was being delayed.
"The principle of serving the arrest warrants still stands but execution of the warrants is being delayed in view of the prospect of resolving the current situation with dialogue," he told Reuters.
Prosecutors had previously said the union bosses would be arrested if they did not halt industrial action immediately.
Nevertheless, police have so far picked up five of the 20 unionists who have warrants outstanding for their arrest.
Confederation president Kwon Young-kil said on Saturday he had decided to halt indefinite strikes against the labour law and would limit stoppages to one day every week on Wednesdays.
The law makes it easier for companies to lay off workers and replace strikers. President Kim says labour reform is necessary to cut corporate costs and improve competitiveness.

Kim's talks with opposition figures would follow meetings with religious leaders, including the heads of the influential Roman Catholic and Protestant churches, who urged the president to seek a peaceful solution.
Opposition politicians who have insisted the law be scrapped have thrown their weight behind the unions.

Police maintained a tight noose around Myongdong. A team of 10 world labour leaders headed by Bill Jordan of the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions is scheduled to visit the cathedral on Monday.
They will replace a team of four international union leaders who were hustled out of Seoul last week after deportation threats.
Seoul's top immigration official has said the new delegation would be expelled if it joined strike-related protests.
